# Introduction

Forecasting tools can make it easy to generate predictions, but understanding how they work helps us decide when to rely on them. Different workloads have different patterns, and a model that works well for one may be less useful for another. In this post, I'll explore two forecasting approaches in R and test how well they predict phone volume.

Accurate phone forecasts can help teams balance phone coverage with other work and plan time for training, staff meetings, or system updates. Here, I'll use hourly counts of recorded inquiries to New York City's 311 call center to explore daily, weekly, and yearly patterns and test predictions against later observations.

I'll start with Prophet, which models trends and recurring patterns and can incorporate holidays or other predictors. Then I'll explore ETS (Error, Trend, Seasonality), an exponential smoothing approach that gives more weight to recent observations. I'll compare their predictions against actual call volumes and finish with a recommendation for this dataset, including the limitations of that comparison.

# Set-up

Before building the forecasts, I'll load the packages and bring in the data we'll use throughout the analysis.

I'll use tidyverse and lubridate to prepare the data, httr2 to download it, Prophet and ETS to forecast volume.

```{r setup}
#| eval: true
#| code-fold: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false

library(tidyverse)
library(lubridate)
library(httr2)
library(prophet)
library(forecast)
```

The [NYC 311 Call Center Inquiry dataset](https://data.cityofnewyork.us/City-Government/311-Call-Center-Inquiry/wewp-mm3p/about_data) records agent-handled inquiries. I'll download hourly counts for 2015–2018, using the first three years for training and 2018 for testing. These counts exclude abandoned calls, and missing hours may not mean zero activity. This period also avoids pandemic-related underreporting beginning in March 2020.

```{r data}
#| eval: true
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Show Code"
#| warning: false
#| message: false

response <- request("https://data.cityofnewyork.us/resource/wewp-mm3p.csv") |>
  req_url_query(
    `$select` = "date_trunc_ymd(date_time) AS date, date_extract_hh(date_time) AS hour, count(*) AS inquiry_count",
    `$where` = "date_time >= '2015-01-01T00:00:00' AND date_time < '2019-01-01T00:00:00'",
    `$group` = "date,hour",
    `$order` = "date,hour",
    `$limit` = 100000
  ) |>
  req_timeout(180) |>
  req_perform()

data <- read_csv(I(resp_body_string(response)), show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  mutate(date = as_date(date))
```

# Explore the Data

The first six rows show the three fields we'll use: `date` identifies weekdays and separates our training and testing periods, `hour` lets us focus on 8 a.m.–5 p.m., and `inquiry_count` is the recorded volume we'll summarize and forecast. We'll focus on Monday–Friday. Because the counts reflect inquiries handled by agents, they may understate demand when callers hang up before reaching someone, which matters if we use the forecast to plan phone coverage.

```{r preview-data}
#| eval: true
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Show Code"
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 2.8
#| fig-alt: "First six rows of the hourly inquiry data, showing date, hour, and inquiry count."

preview <- head(data) |>
  mutate(
    row = row_number(),
    date = format(date, "%Y-%m-%d"),
    hour = as.character(hour),
    inquiry_count = scales::comma(inquiry_count)
  ) |>
  pivot_longer(-row, names_to = "field", values_to = "value") |>
  mutate(field = factor(field, levels = c("date", "hour", "inquiry_count")))

headers <- tibble(
  field = factor(
    c("date", "hour", "inquiry_count"),
    levels = c("date", "hour", "inquiry_count")
  ),
  value = c("date", "hour", "inquiry_count")
)

ggplot(preview, aes(x = field, y = -row)) +
  geom_tile(aes(fill = row %% 2 == 0), color = "#F5F3EF", linewidth = 0.6) +
  geom_text(aes(label = value), family = "serif", color = "#283438", size = 4) +
  geom_tile(
    data = headers, aes(x = field, y = 0),
    inherit.aes = FALSE, fill = "#24434A", color = "#F5F3EF"
  ) +
  geom_text(
    data = headers, aes(x = field, y = 0, label = value),
    inherit.aes = FALSE, family = "serif",
    fontface = "bold", color = "white", size = 4
  ) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("FALSE" = "#F5F3EF", "TRUE" = "#E3E9E7")) +
  scale_x_discrete(expand = c(0, 0)) +
  scale_y_continuous(expand = c(0, 0)) +
  theme_void() +
  theme(
    legend.position = "none",
    plot.background = element_rect(fill = "#F5F3EF", color = NA),
    plot.margin = margin(8, 8, 8, 8)
  )
```
